title: Elon Musk Just Threatened the Coming Democratic Majority
author: Lee Hepner
content:
A few months ago, Paramount owner David Ellison succeeded in forcing
California and Democratic states attorneys general to drop their antitrust
suit against his acquisition of Warner Brothers. He used a variety of tactics,
including a threat to move the studios out of the state, and ultimately
bluffed the elected officials into folding. BIG
[predicted](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/monopoly-round-up-the-threat-
to-move) at the time that Ellison's threatened capital strike, along with
political coercion, was a _preview_ of what is to come if voters choose
Democrats as a Congressional majority.

And sure enough, that's what one of Ellison's close allies - Elon Musk - just
did. Earlier this week, following reports that Musk had throttled Ukraine's
access to his Starlink satellite network, Politico ran a
[story](https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2026/10/20/congress/dem-gavels-
elon-musk-01127662) that several Dem members of Congress are gearing up to
hold oversight hearings if the midterms go their way in a couple of weeks.

Musk responded by explicitly threatening any Democrat or institution seeking
to scrutinize him, his portfolio of companies, or his time at DOGE. Here's
what he said:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!mKDD!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4c4ddac1-113a-4be8-aa04-310326decb5e_887x395.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!mKDD!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4c4ddac1-113a-4be8-aa04-310326decb5e_887x395.png)

It's a remarkable statement, and it speaks to a fundamental view held by Musk
and his allies that the votes of ordinary people simply should not count. He
and a small circle make the key decisions in our society.

Musk tweets so much that it's hard to keep track of his views, but he is also
explicit about that point too:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Z2pz!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F97424355-1390-4f3b-b4d3-5f9febcb0c13_1159x1523.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Z2pz!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F97424355-1390-4f3b-b4d3-5f9febcb0c13_1159x1523.jpeg)

Musk's political threats are not really the story. The story is that he
actually has the leverage to make them real, through a network of political
influence and, more importantly, control over key social infrastructure. As
with Ellison's ability to harm California, Musk can actually threaten the
Pentagon, foreign countries, and the U.S. government itself. And he does.

The story is that, depending on the outcome of the midterms, which we'll know
a lot more about in 11 days, we're entering a new phase of a battle between
democratic systems and oligarchical ones that will test the limits of Musk's
extraordinary power and the temerity of Democrats to actually do something
about it.

[![Twitter advertisers say they're worried about Elon Musk's tweets and  actions | Vox](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!U31Z!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fad2f4a68-dc03-4334-acee-cc604622b39d_2400x1587.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!U31Z!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fad2f4a68-dc03-4334-acee-cc604622b39d_2400x1587.jpeg)

### The Fool on the Hill

Let's start by reckoning with Musk's power, which spans all sorts of
infrastructure, campaign finance, and media. As to his control over critical
infrastructure, the most salient revelation, and the catalyst for renewed
political controversy, is Musk's apparent role in
[throttling](https://www.wsj.com/world/ukraine-starlink-elon-musk-trump-
dbc49193) Ukraine's access to military-grade satellite service through
Starlink, a satellite-based internet network operated by Musk's aerospace
company, SpaceX. Ukraine took significant damage and was unable to orchestrate
its offensive strategy against Russia as a result of the cut-off.

How does this system organize the fate of wars? Starlink is adjacent to
Starshield, a SpaceX service that provides secure communications for
governments. It's a critical piece of national security infrastructure. And
that goes beyond providing internet access to war-torn battlefields.

By some accounts, Starlink operates roughly 75% of all active maneuverable
satellites. It provides internet service designed to connect homes,
businesses, vehicles, ships, aircraft, and more, including in remote locations
that are poorly served by existing broadband or fiber-optic cables.

And it's increasingly important commercially. Just yesterday, United CEO Scott
Kirby [cited](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/technology/tech-news/united-
airlines-ceo-is-very-happy-with-airlines-deal-with-starlink-says-helping-us-
get-customers-elon-musk-responds/articleshow/135111155.cms) the airline's
partnership with Starlink for boosting its market share. (To believe this, you
have to believe there's actually enough competition between airlines for
Starlink to make a difference, and I have my doubts, but it's clearly a useful
service.)

SpaceX has private shareholders, but it is a government sanctioned firm whose
growth over the past two decades is fundamentally owed to public funds, some
$48 billion in contracts, loans, subsidies and tax credits, as well as access
to key public space infrastructure. SpaceX started receiving DARPA money in
2003, a year after SpaceX was formed, and has been a go-to private contractor
for every administration since. In other words, Musk's control over essential
infrastructure, and his ability to wield it privately despite procurement
terms superficially nodding to safeguards, is a bipartisan creation of the
federal government.

There is some debate over the extent to which Musk wields that power
unilaterally or in collaboration with government officials -- it's far closer
to a public-private partnership than a purely private entity -- and a 2023
[expose](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2023/08/28/elon-musks-shadow-rule)
by Ronan Farrow reveals how that collaboration looks more like dependence
across swaths of the federal government:

> Current and former officials from NASA, the Department of Defense, the
> Department of Transportation, the Federal Aviation Administration, and the
> Occupational Safety and Health Administration told me that Musk's influence
> had become inescapable in their work, and several of them said that they now
> treat him like a sort of unelected official. One Pentagon spokesman said
> that he was keeping Musk apprised of [Farrow's] inquiries about his role in
> Ukraine and would grant an interview with an official about the matter only
> with Musk's permission. "We'll talk to you if Elon wants us to," he told
> [Farrow]. In a podcast interview last year, Musk was asked whether he has
> more influence than the American government. He replied immediately, "In
> some ways."

Not unlike other historical and contemporary barons of distribution networks,
from Cornelius Vanderbilt to Jay Gould to Andrew Mellon to Jeff Bezos, Musk's
control over infrastructure provides him with leverage over public
institutions. His quasi-unilateral intervention in the Ukraine-Russia conflict
is one example. And the way that power works is by threatening to pull the
deployment of that infrastructure, or discriminate between who can access it,
which has commercial and geopolitical implications. It's the power of a
capital strike, not unlike Meta's [renewed
threat](https://x.com/FrancisBrennan/status/2112983270434484308?s=20), just
yesterday, to cut off service to the State of New Mexico in response to a jury
verdict finding them liable for over 43 million violations of the state's
unfair practices law. Or [take](https://www.wired.com/story/amazon-tussles-
with-seattle-as-it-seeks-a-second-home/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) (Amazon)
[your](https://www.theverge.com/2024/4/12/24128363/google-cjpa-news-removal-
california) (Google) [pick](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/08/14/uber-lyft-
threaten-to-suspend-service-in-california-that-may-backfire.html) (Uber/Lyft),
really, because capital strikes are as American as unbridled monopoly power.

Musk's threat is also to use his wealth, so much of which is traceable to
benefits conferred by the government, to distort our democratic elections.
Bloomberg's Billionaires Index estimates that SpaceX is the source of over
[75%](https://www.bloomberg.com/billionaires/profiles/elon-r-musk/) of Musk's
overall net worth, which hovers around $1 trillion. And Musk's election
spending is a business investment for which he expects a return. As of mid-
October, nearly 50 megadonors had spent close to $2.4 billion on the midterm
elections, and Musk's [$369
million](https://www.washingtonpost.com/elections/interactive/2026/06/25/these-
are-biggest-individual-donors-2026-election-cycle/) in campaign contributions
dwarfs everyone else. At least $176.8 million has gone solely to support Texas
AG Ken Paxton's bid for the Senate and to oppose Democrat candidate James
Talarico.

Musk is far from the first, or only, oligarch to wield other instruments of
persuasion, including the media. His purchase of Twitter/X evokes Henry Ford's
1919 purchase of the Dearborn Independent, then the second most widely
distributed newspaper behind the New York Times, in the wake of his Senate
campaign loss. And just as Henry Ford used his newspaper to grind various
political axes, with a heavy dose of overt antisemitism, Musk's takeover of
Twitter has [amplified](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10098-2)
partisan conservative voices and driven social wedge issues to divert
attention from a more unifying politics.

Add to Musk's efforts to control the public commons his
[lawsuit](https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-
courts/ca5/25-10630/25-10630-2026-08-21.html) against Media Matters, alleging
that the watchdog group interfered with Twitter/X contracts and economic
advantage when it published a report showing advertisements appearing next to
pro-Nazi content. Understandably, many advertisers pulled their spending from
Musk's platform. Here, Musk's effort to censor his opponents is also a threat
to bury any other opponent in litigation costs. And it's yet another data
point in Musk's leverage over the federal government, reflected in the Trump
administration's transparent weaponization of antitrust. The FTC's own,
subsequent
[investigation](https://www.washingtonpost.com/style/media/2025/06/23/media-
matters-ftc-lawsuit/) into Media Matters is hard to see as anything but the
abuse of public resources at Musk's behest.

### Ladies and Gentlemen, the Democrats!

But of course, Musk and the billionaires are one part of the equation. The
other is voters, who are choosing to move away from DOGE and the Trump era by
voting for the ostensible opposition party. And what are some of those
Democrats likely to do? That's less clear.

One response is to campaign on the blatant corruption eroding our democracy,
as Talarico is doing. Multiple studies have observed that ad saturation driven
by massive campaign spending can have [marginal
returns](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/15377857.2021.1997877) on
voter persuasion and eventually lead to [voter
suppression](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0261379418300374).
And on some level, voters react to the source of funds. A recent Data for
Progress [poll](https://www.dataforprogress.org/blog/2026/7/28/aipac-ai-and-
crypto-funded-democrats-underperform-democrats-who-reject-corporate-pac-money)
showed that 75% of likely voters were less likely to vote for candidates who
receive support from the AI industry. Musk is polarizing, at best, and has a
[net-negative](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/elon-musk-texas-
senate-race-republicans-rcna596670) favorability rating even in Texas.

A different response, one we saw with the Skydance merger, is to cower and
fold before the superrich. For example, even though support for AI - another
area of Musk investment - has become a third rail in politics, some Democrats
are [backing away](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/17/democrats-ai-
regulation-midterms-warnings-01082564) from talking about it at all:

> Senior Democrats and candidates are worried that if they go too hard in
> criticizing AI, industry-affiliated super PACs could[ drop millions more
> dollars against them](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/03/ai-crypto-
> super-pac-spending-primaries-01062929), according to interviews with more
> than a dozen Democratic lawmakers and strategists. They are especially
> worried about a slate of competitive races, including Reps. Don Davis in
> North Carolina, Marcy Kaptur in Ohio, Henry Cuellar in Texas and a handful
> of South Texas and Pennsylvania races, getting hit with even more spending
> on topics like AI.

I have experience in politics and in running large legislative campaigns, so
here I'll offer advice. Be direct and aggressive against men like Musk.
Politicians don't need to chase every polarizing issue, but the inability to
put forward an honest and moral position on a defining economic and social
question kneecaps the ability to harness broader political support.

And we can see that because Republicans increasingly want Musk's money, but
[don't want him](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/elon-musk-
texas-senate-race-republicans-rcna596670) near their campaigns. Musk's
donations are funneled through political action committees like the Senate
Leadership Committee, America First, and Lone Star Liberty, none of which bear
his name. And while Republicans have been far less critical overall of Musk's
political interloping, several spoke out against his DOGE cuts, and Rep. Mike
Turner of Ohio has [joined](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/ukraine-starlink-
republicans-mike-turner-kevin-cramer-face-the-nation/) calls for an oversight
hearing on Musk's weaponization of Starlink in Ukraine. Republicans are
constrained by Musk's giving to form a more coherent political message.
Democrats shouldn't be.

### **The Government Gave, and the Government Can Take Away**

Here's my prediction. I don't think Dems will back down from their calls for
oversight hearings regarding Musk's conduct. And I suspect some Republicans
will join, particularly if Dems overperform in the midterms. The fact about
people like Elon Musk is that their power is also their weakness. Campaign
consultants can hardly beg for a more perfect foil than someone whose most
identifiable consumer product, the Cybertruck, is a politically charged
purchase and a visual manifestation of ego.

But it would be naive, if not damaging, to think that oversight hearings are
adequate on their own. Oversight hearings easily drift into theatrical content
farms, and viral social media clips, on their own, risk reinforcing a growing
perception that too many Democrats are more adept at pretending to care than
doing anything meaningful to generate durable outcomes.

More importantly, the question isn't whether there should be oversight, but
the point of that oversight. It's critical to neutralize Musk's ability to
threaten nation-states and our own government, and if that means building the
case for breaking apart his empire or imposing new rules, that must be baked
into the hearings from the beginning. A free society cannot be bullied by
threats of capital strikes, particularly as to essential infrastructure, and
the ability to channel capital must be done through democratic means.

What would real oversight of oligarchs look like? Well, it would mean seeking
intel about corrupt slush funds for the White House ballroom or Trump's
presidential library, about the purchase of equity stakes in companies like
[Anduril](https://www.forbes.com/sites/saradorn/2026/10/09/abc-article-on-
trumps-sons-pentagon-linked-investments-removed-after-it-was-published-
prematurely/) just before receiving nearly $1.8 billion in government
contracts, about leading a $300 million investment in
[Polymarket](https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/donald-trump-jr-s-fund-
boosts-polymarket-investment-by-around-300-million-45270bba) while it receives
conspicuously favorable regulatory treatment, or about $2.6 billion in stock
trades immediately prior to the [Iran
war](https://liccardo.house.gov/media/in-the-news/house-dem-sam-liccardo-
probes-suspicious-oil-trades-during-iran-war). It would also mean
simultaneously governing, by moving legislation to close the _McDonnell_
["official acts"](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/10/constitution-
trump-doj-supreme-court-corruption/689042/) loophole, to ban [profiting off of
public service](https://www.warren.senate.gov/wp-
content/uploads/media/doc/Master%20Summary%20of%20Anti%20Corruption%20Act%20-%20FINAL.pdf),
and to ban [Congressional stock trading](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-
congress/house-bill/7008). When the next President takes office, Congress
should abandon the filibuster to do these things. The path to durable
governance is through tearing down parliamentary barriers to governing.

Moreover, oversight hearings cannot stop at the low hanging fruit. Democrats
must create a drumbeat for oversight of corporate bad actors. It's a target-
rich market: JetBlue and Instacart on surveillance pricing, Live Nation
inducing a corrupt settlement with the Justice Department amid their losing
antitrust trial, Skydance on its relationship to sovereign wealth funds, Jeff
Bezos and Amazon on their ongoing monopolization of e-commerce, HPE-Juniper on
the circumstances of their corrupt merger settlement, the Big Three PBMs, the
Big Four Meatpackers, KKR and Black Bear on private equity crippling youth
sports, Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic on the efforts to hide the private
financial risk of the AI bubble in a systemically vulnerable network of
private credit, insurance, pension funds and banks. And on and on.

And Elon Musk. The richest welfare recipient in the world. As to Musk, the
most obvious thing to do is not a matter of partisan convenience, but of
strategic necessity: nationalize SpaceX. It's something Matt has [written
about for BIG previously](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/steve-bannon-
nationalize-spacex). SpaceX should be treated like a public utility. It's a
private company in form, but hardly so in terms of the government funding that
has been central to its growth.

Will Democrats actually accomplish real oversight? I don't know. But I can say
that squandering power breeds resentment, and fear of reprisal is an
abdication of the duty to govern.

Fundamentally, Musk's threat, "Live by the sword, die by the sword," is a
cautionary admonition against violence, taken from scripture, Matthew 26:52.
Perhaps the best response draws from another scripture, Job 1:21, "The Lord
gave, and the Lord hath taken away."
